Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Minneapolis, USA - Museum Tour

Stop 1: Self-portrait with Dr Arrieta

Address: 2400 3rd Ave S, Minneapolis, MN 55404

Coordinates: 44.9737, -93.2591

Museum Information:

The museum is open daily except Monday. Admission is free.

Orientation: These diverse works united by their exploration of the human psyche await your discovery. Your first stop is Self-portrait with Dr Arrieta. The flicker of light on canvas catches your eye—stand close enough to see the brushstrokes of "Self-portrait with Dr Arrieta," just beyond arm’s reach, where the contrasts between pallid skin and deep shadow become clear. From here, Goya’s weakened body and Dr. Arrieta’s steady hand emerge with striking immediacy; the intimacy of their exchange is most vivid when you can read the gratitude and exhaustion in their faces.

Late in 1819, at seventy-three years of age, Francisco Goya survived a severe, life-threatening illness under the care of his physician, Dr. Eugenio García Arrieta. Though Goya had previously satirized doctors in his artwork as dishonest and inept, he painted this portrait in 1820 as a personal gift of gratitude for the doctor who saved his life. By dedicating this oil on canvas painting to Arrieta, Goya marked a significant change in his artistic expression, turning away from grand public statements to something deeply private. The painting itself shows Goya, gaunt and pale, supported in bed by Dr. The doctor’s face is composed and focused, his arm gently steadying Goya. The canvas is alive with the tension between fragility and devotion. Goya’s choice of oil paint allows him to build up translucent layers in the flesh, giving the skin a waxy, almost feverish pallor—there is nothing idealized here. The background plunges into shadow, isolating the two men; the world outside seems to recede, leaving only the moment of crisis and care. This work was created shortly after Goya survived his illness, which lends the image a raw vulnerability. What stands out to many is the way Goya casts himself not as a heroic survivor, but as a patient—helpless, grateful, utterly dependent on Arrieta’s skill and kindness.

Directions: Continue through Minneapolis Institute of Art — next is Lobster Telephone.

Stop 2: Lobster Telephone

Address: 2400 3rd Ave S, Minneapolis, MN 55404

Coordinates: 44.9737, -93.2591

Orientation: Stand just to the side of Lobster Telephone, so that the arc of the plaster lobster stretching across the black Bakelite receiver comes into full view.

British poet and collector Edward James commissioned Salvador Dalí to create eleven lobster telephones for his collection in 1936. The inspiration struck that same year when Dalí, James, and their companions were eating lobsters together and an empty shell accidentally landed across a nearby telephone. James installed versions of the piece at Monkton, his country house in West Sussex. As a result, the Lobster Telephone became an iconic piece, eventually finding its way to the National Galleries of Scotland, where it continues to captivate audiences with its whimsical yet thought-provoking design. The object before you is a Surrealist construction: a real, functioning black Bakelite telephone, its receiver capped not by the expected earpiece, but by a pale, plaster lobster in place of the handset. The lobster’s claws reach forward where a mouth might press, its tail curled where a hand would grasp. Dalí’s choice of materials—plaster for the lobster, Bakelite for the telephone—was deliberate. Bakelite, a hallmark of modern industrial design in the 1930s, stands in stark contrast to the soft, organic curves of the crustacean. This object was more than a joke or a provocation. James, a prominent collector of Surrealist art, commissioned various versions of the Lobster Telephone in both color and white. Their partnership marked a significant shift: Surrealism, previously confined to canvases and poems, now permeated everyday spaces. The telephone ceased to be merely a communication tool—it was metamorphosed into something disconcerting, even absurd. Standing here, the effect is immediate. Lobster Telephone feels playful, yet there is a tension—an unease—in the way mouth meets claw, the way the familiar becomes alien. In this piece, the passage of time is measured not by brushstrokes, but by the slow, persistent intrusion of the subconscious into the rooms of the everyday.

Directions: Your final stop in Minneapolis Institute of Art: Melencolia I.

Stop 3: Melencolia I

Address: 2400 3rd Ave S, Minneapolis, MN 55404

Coordinates: 44.9737, -93.2591

Orientation: As you stand here, lean in just enough to see the faint, meticulous lines of Albrecht Dürer’s Melencolia I—especially the shadowed area beneath the winged figure’s elbow. From this close vantage, the engraved marks reveal their astonishing density, each one deliberate, forming the somber folds of her robe and the scattered geometric instruments. Standing here, the composition tightens; the enigmatic mood is heightened, and the technical precision of the 1514 engraving comes into sharp focus.

In 1936, the Minneapolis Institute of Art acquired Albrecht Dürer’s engraving, Melencolia I. Before this acquisition, the piece had been part of various private collections, its enigmatic imagery inspiring countless interpretations over the centuries. By securing the engraving, the museum not only preserved a significant work of art but also made it accessible to a broader public audience, allowing for continued study and appreciation. As a result, Melencolia I became an integral part of the museum’s collection, contributing to its reputation as a custodian of Renaissance art and providing visitors with a direct connection to Dürer’s mastery. Nearly a century after Dürer created Melencolia I, Jan Wierix, active in the Netherlands, produced an exact copy of the engraving. Wierix’s decision to replicate Dürer’s work speaks to the engraving’s considerable influence and reach; it was not only admired but deemed worthy of painstaking reproduction by another accomplished engraver. As Wierix’s version circulated, Melencolia I’s ambiguous symbols and psychological depth entered new contexts, shaping how later artists and collectors perceived Dürer’s original. Melencolia I is a large engraving on paper—about 9 1/2 by 7 5/16 inches—created in 1514. The central subject is a winged, melancholic female figure, her gaze cast downward, surrounded by geometric instruments and enigmatic objects. The choice of engraving as a medium allowed Dürer to achieve a level of precision and subtlety in line that amplifies the sense of psychological tension. This work is often read as a reflection of the intellectual artist’s state—a kind of spiritual self-portrait—where reason and imagination coexist uncomfortably. Standing before Melencolia I, the sense of introspection is almost palpable. Here, the stakes are different: Dürer’s engraving holds the tension between order and uncertainty, offering no easy answers but instead the honest labor of creative struggle. In this space, the museum becomes not just a collection of objects but a site where clarity and chaos are held in careful balance.

This tour reveals the tension between personal experience and broader artistic expression, as seen in works like Self-portrait with Dr Arrieta. This exploration encourages us to reflect on how art serves as a medium for vulnerability, creativity, and the complexities of the human condition. That's 3 stops in all.
